title: Dental Calculus & Other Predisposing Factors — Test

mcqs.q: Dental calculus is best defined as:
opts: Mineralized bacterial plaque on natural teeth and dental prostheses
A soft white deposit removed by rinsing
An acquired pellicle of salivary glycoproteins
mcqs.explain: Calculus is mineralized plaque; the primary cause of gingival inflammation remains bacterial plaque, with calculus acting as a predisposing factor.

mcqs.q: The source of minerals for SUPRAgingival calculus is:
mcqs.explain: Supragingival (salivary) calculus mineralizes from saliva; subgingival (serumal) calculus mineralizes from gingival crevicular fluid.

mcqs.q: Supragingival calculus is most commonly found on the:
opts: Buccal surfaces of maxillary molars and lingual surfaces of mandibular anteriors
Palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors only
mcqs.explain: These sites lie opposite the openings of the salivary ducts (parotid and submandibular/sublingual).

mcqs.q: The typical colour and consistency of SUBgingival calculus is:
opts: Dark brown or greenish-black, hard and dense, firmly attached
White or whitish-yellow, clay-like and easily detached
mcqs.explain: Supragingival calculus is white/whitish-yellow, hard and clay-like and easily detached; subgingival is dark, dense and firmly attached.

mcqs.q: When the gingival tissues recede, subgingival calculus:
mcqs.explain: Its classification depends on its position relative to the gingival margin, so recession exposes it.

mcqs.q: The inorganic content of supragingival calculus constitutes:
mcqs.explain: The remainder is organic; two-thirds of the inorganic component is crystalline in structure.

mcqs.q: The MOST abundant crystal form in calculus is:
mcqs.explain: Hydroxyapatite 58%, magnesium whitlockite 21%, octacalcium phosphate 12%, brushite 9%.

mcqs.q: Brushite is found predominantly in the:
mcqs.explain: Brushite predominates in the mandibular anterior region, whereas magnesium whitlockite predominates in posterior areas.

mcqs.q: Hydroxyapatite and octacalcium phosphate are found in what proportion of all supragingival calculus?
mcqs.explain: These two crystal forms are near-universal in supragingival calculus.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE of the organic content of calculus?
opts: Protein–polysaccharide complexes, epithelial cells, leukocytes and microorganisms
It is composed purely of lipid material
It makes up 70–90% of the whole deposit
mcqs.explain: Organic content includes carbohydrates (1.9–9.1%), salivary proteins (5.9–8.2%) and lipids (0.2%).

mcqs.q: Which feature distinguishes subgingival from supragingival calculus in composition?
opts: Salivary proteins are ABSENT in subgingival calculus
Salivary proteins are present in both equally
mcqs.explain: Subgingival calculus has more magnesium whitlockite, less brushite/octacalcium phosphate, and no salivary proteins.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the described modes of calculus attachment to the tooth?
opts: Chemical bonding to enamel hydroxyapatite by covalent bonds
Attachment by an organic pellicle on cementum and enamel
Penetration of bacterial calculus into cementum
mcqs.explain: The four modes are pellicle attachment, mechanical locking into irregularities (caries, resorption lacunae), penetration into cementum, and close adaptation of the undersurface to cemental depressions.

mcqs.q: Calculus formation begins between:
opts: The 1st and 14th day of plaque formation
mcqs.explain: It is 50% mineralized in 2 days and 60–90% mineralized in 12 days, though not all plaque necessarily calcifies.

mcqs.q: Plaque is what degree mineralized after 2 days?
mcqs.explain: 50% in 2 days; 60–90% by 12 days.

mcqs.q: The calcium content of plaque compared with saliva is:
mcqs.explain: Additionally, the early plaque of heavy calculus formers contains three times more phosphorus, suggesting phosphorus may be more critical for mineralization.

mcqs.q: Calculus accumulation reaches a maximal level in about:
mcqs.explain: After this there is a decline in accumulation known as the reversal phenomenon.

mcqs.q: The 'reversal phenomenon' is explained by:
opts: Mechanical wear of bulky calculus from food, cheeks, lips and tongue
Reabsorption of calcium by the tooth
mcqs.explain: Bulky calculus becomes vulnerable to mechanical wear, so accumulation declines after its peak.

mcqs.q: Which factor is proposed to cause a local rise in saturation of calcium and phosphate ions?
opts: A rise in the pH of saliva
mcqs.explain: Theory 1 cites a rise in pH, colloidal proteins in saliva, and enzymes such as phosphatase and esterase.

mcqs.q: The theory in which seeding agents induce small foci of calcification that enlarge and coalesce is called:
mcqs.explain: Seeding agents nucleate mineral that grows and coalesces into a calcified mass. Heterogeneous nucleation.

mcqs.q: Current opinion regarding the role of bacteria in calculus mineralization is that they are:
opts: Only passively involved and simply calcified with other plaque components
The active initiators of all crystal growth
mcqs.explain: Mineralization starts extracellularly around both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms and spreads until matrix and bacteria are calcified.

mcqs.q: The main etiologic significance of calculus is that it:
opts: A fixed nidus holding plaque against the gingiva, making removal difficult
It directly releases endotoxin that destroys bone
It is itself the primary cause of gingivitis
It prevents plaque from ever reaching the sulcus
mcqs.explain: Calculus is always covered with non-mineralized plaque; its removal along with subgingival plaque is the cornerstone of periodontal therapy.

mcqs.q: Subgingival calculus is best regarded as:
opts: A product of deep pockets as well as a contributing factor
The sole initiating cause of periodontitis
A protective barrier over the root
mcqs.explain: Deep pockets favour its formation, and it then perpetuates plaque retention.

mcqs.q: Iatrogenic factors in periodontics are defined as:
opts: Inadequate dental procedures that contribute to deterioration of the periodontal tissues
mcqs.explain: They include faults of margin location, marginal gap, contour, occlusion, materials, the restorative procedure and RPD design.

mcqs.q: A gap of what size between a subgingival restoration margin and the unprepared tooth permits plaque colonization?
mcqs.explain: Even this small marginal discrepancy is colonized by bacterial plaque.

mcqs.q: Which restoration margin location is associated with the GREATEST plaque formation and most severe gingivitis?
mcqs.explain: Subgingival margins cause greater plaque, more severe gingivitis, deeper pockets and a change in microflora; supragingival margins give health similar to non-restored surfaces.

mcqs.q: Overcontoured crowns are harmful because they:
opts: Accumulate plaque and prevent self-cleaning by the cheek, lips and tongue
mcqs.explain: Undercontoured crowns do not retain as much plaque; failure to re-establish interproximal embrasures causes papillary inflammation.

mcqs.q: A 'plunger cusp' contributes to periodontal damage by:
opts: Forcibly wedging food into the interproximal embrasure
mcqs.explain: Food impaction is the forceful wedging of food into the periodontium by occlusal forces; light/open contacts and excessive anterior overbite also contribute.

mcqs.q: Which restorative material is specifically noted as injurious to the periodontal tissues?
mcqs.explain: Materials are generally not injurious except self-curing acrylics; pontic undersurfaces should barely touch the mucosa.

mcqs.q: Removable partial dentures harm the periodontium particularly when they:
opts: Cover the gingival tissue and are worn day and night
mcqs.explain: They favour plaque accumulation, promote emergence of spirochetal microorganisms, and require careful personalized oral hygiene instruction.

mcqs.q: Forceful packing of a gingival retraction cord may cause:
opts: Impacted debris left behind, producing a foreign body reaction
mcqs.explain: Rubber dam clamps, matrix bands and burs can also lacerate the gingiva, causing mechanical trauma and inflammation.

mcqs.q: Excessive orthodontic force produces:
opts: Necrosis of the periodontal ligament and adjacent alveolar bone with apical root resorption
mcqs.explain: Moderate forces produce bone remodeling and repair; orthodontics also causes plaque retention with microflora change and gingival trauma.

mcqs.q: Chewing tobacco placed in the mandibular buccal vestibule causes:
opts: Localized recession, attachment loss, leukoplakia and severe periodontitis risk
Generalized gingival enlargement and nothing else
Immediate irreversible pulpitis of the adjacent teeth
An increase in the width of attached gingiva
mcqs.explain: Snuff and chewing tobacco are the two main forms of smokeless tobacco.

mcqs.q: Irradiated bone becomes hypovascular and hypoxic, leading to:
mcqs.explain: Non-restorable teeth or those with significant periodontal problems should be extracted BEFORE radiation therapy to reduce this risk.

mcqs.q: Iatrogenic gingival injuries differ from factitious injuries in that iatrogenic injuries are:
opts: Acute, whereas factitious injuries are more chronic
mcqs.explain: Self-inflicted injuries may be mechanical (toothbrush, toothpicks), chemical (allergy to toothpaste, gum, tobacco) or thermal.

saqs.q: Compare supragingival and subgingival calculus under location, colour, source, consistency and composition.
saqs.a: SUPRAGINGIVAL — coronal to the margin, visible, white/whitish-yellow, from SALIVA, hard and clay-like, easily detached, more brushite and octacalcium phosphate, less magnesium whitlockite, salivary proteins present. SUBGINGIVAL — below the margin, found by tactile exploration, dark brown or greenish-black, from GINGIVAL CREVICULAR FLUID, hard, dense and firmly attached, less brushite and octacalcium phosphate, more magnesium whitlockite, no salivary proteins. When the gingiva recedes, subgingival becomes supragingival.

SUBGINGIVAL
rows: below the margin — detected by careful tactile perception with an explorer
more brushite and octacalcium phosphate, less magnesium whitlockite; salivary proteins present
less brushite and octacalcium phosphate, more magnesium whitlockite; salivary proteins absent

ans.text: When the gingiva recedes, subgingival calculus becomes supragingival.

saqs.q: Describe the composition of calculus, giving the crystal forms and their percentages.
saqs.a: Supragingival calculus is 70–90% inorganic. Crystals: hydroxyapatite 58%, magnesium whitlockite 21%, octacalcium phosphate 12%, brushite 9%; two-thirds of the inorganic part is crystalline. Hydroxyapatite and octacalcium phosphate occur in 97–100%; brushite predominates mandibular anteriorly, whitlockite posteriorly. Organic: protein–polysaccharide complexes, epithelial cells, leukocytes and microorganisms — carbohydrates 1.9–9.1%, salivary proteins 5.9–8.2%, lipids 0.2%.

ans.text: Supragingival calculus is 70–90% inorganic, the remainder organic. The major inorganic components are calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, magnesium phosphate and trace elements; two-thirds of the inorganic component is crystalline.
Hydroxyapatite and octacalcium phosphate occur in 97–100% of all supragingival calculus; brushite predominates in the mandibular anterior region and magnesium whitlockite in posterior areas.

list: Protein–polysaccharide complexes, desquamated epithelial cells, leukocytes and microorganisms

saqs.q: List the four modes of attachment of calculus to the tooth surface.
saqs.a: A) An organic pellicle on cementum and enamel. B) Mechanical locking into surface irregularities such as caries and resorption lacunae. C) Penetration of bacterial calculus into the cementum. D) Close adaptation of the calculus undersurface to depressions on the cementum. These explain why subgingival calculus is firmly attached and hard to remove completely.

list: A — attachment by an organic pellicle on cementum and enamel
B — mechanical locking into surface irregularities such as caries and resorption lacunae
C — penetration of bacterial calculus into the cementum
D — close adaptation of the undersurface of the calculus to depressions on the cementum

ans.text: These modes explain why subgingival calculus is firmly attached and difficult to remove completely.

saqs.q: Describe calculus formation and the theories of its mineralization.
saqs.a: Starts between day 1 and 14 of plaque formation; 50% mineralized in 2 days, 60–90% in 12 days. Plaque calcium is 2–20× saliva; heavy formers' early plaque has 3× more phosphorus, so phosphorus may be more critical. Calcium binds the organic matrix, then calcium phosphate precipitates. Peaks at 10 weeks to 6 months, then declines — the REVERSAL PHENOMENON, from mechanical wear. THEORIES: (1) mineral precipitation from local supersaturation (pH rise, colloidal proteins, phosphatase and esterase); (2) seeding agents — the epitactic concept / heterogeneous nucleation. Bacteria are thought to be passively calcified.

list: Starts between the 1st and 14th day of plaque formation
Plaque is 50% mineralized in 2 days and 60–90% in 12 days — though not all plaque necessarily calcifies
Plaque calcium is 2–20× that of saliva; early plaque of heavy calculus formers has three times more phosphorus than calcium and potassium, so phosphorus may be more critical
Calcium binds the protein–carbohydrate complexes of the organic matrix, then calcium phosphate crystals precipitate
Peaks at about 10 weeks to 6 months, then accumulation declines — the 'reversal phenomenon', because bulky calculus is vulnerable to mechanical wear from food and from the cheeks, lips and tongue

saqs.q: Discuss the role of iatrogenic factors in periodontal disease.
saqs.a: Iatrogenic factors are inadequate dental procedures that damage the periodontium. Key characteristics: margin location, the marginal gap, contour, occlusion, materials, the procedure itself and RPD design. Overhangs change the ecologic balance and block cleaning; a 20–40 μm gap allows colonization. Subgingival margins give more plaque, worse gingivitis, deeper pockets and altered flora; equigingival less; supragingival near-normal. Overcontouring accumulates plaque; undercontouring retains less. Materials are generally harmless except self-curing acrylics. Dentures favour plaque, especially worn day and night. Clamps, matrix bands and burs lacerate gingiva; forced retraction cord leaves debris and a foreign body reaction.

ans.text: Iatrogenic factors are inadequate dental procedures that contribute to deterioration of the periodontal tissues.

saqs.q: Outline the other local predisposing factors: malocclusion, orthodontic therapy, habits, tobacco and radiation.
saqs.a: MALOCCLUSION — harder plaque control; prominent roots, high frena and inadequate attached gingiva give recession; tongue thrusting and mouth breathing spread and tilt anteriors with open bite. ORTHODONTICS — plaque retention and flora change; gingival trauma and effects on bone height; moderate force remodels, excessive force necroses PDL and bone with apical root resorption. HABITS — mechanical trauma, chemical irritation, accidental and iatrogenic injury (acute) vs factitious (chronic). SMOKELESS TOBACCO — localized recession, attachment loss, leukoplakia, severe periodontitis. RADIATION — cytotoxic, hypovascular hypoxic bone, osteoradionecrosis; extract compromised teeth before radiotherapy.
